items.prompt: According to this unit, what makes a design decision fall into the category this unit is about, rather than an everyday design choice?
choices: It's expensive to reverse and will be lived with by people who never had the context the original author had
It uses more advanced language features than usual
It was made by the most senior engineer on the team
It took longer than a day to decide
items.explanation: The defining traits are cost-to-reverse and outliving the author's presence to explain it — not seniority of the decider, feature-usage sophistication, or how long the decision took to make. A quick, cheap-to-reverse decision made by a staff engineer doesn't qualify; a hard-to-reverse decision made by anyone does.
items.reference:
🗓️ Renata rotates off in 6 months
🔁 The real question: can a stranger safely change this later
items.learnMore: This unit is about decisions with two compounding properties: they're costly to reverse, and the people who'll live with them won't have the context the decider had. Either alone is manageable — a costly-to-reverse decision made by someone sticking around can still be explained in person; a cheap decision inherited by a stranger barely matters. Both together is what raises the stakes.

items.prompt: Renata is choosing a design for a feature she expects to personally maintain and extend for the next three years, with no team changes planned. How much does this unit's framing apply to that decision?
choices: Much less — the core risk this unit targets is inheritance by someone without the original context, which isn't present here
Exactly the same amount, regardless of who maintains it
More, because staying on the project means more people will eventually touch it
This unit's framing never applies unless multiple teams are involved
items.explanation: The specific risk this unit addresses is a decision being inherited by someone who lacks the original context. If the same person who made the decision is still there to explain and adjust it, that particular risk is much smaller — though not zero, since plans to stay change, and 'three years, no changes planned' is itself an assumption worth being honest about.
items.reference:
🗓️ Renata rotates off in 6 months
🔁 The real question: can a stranger safely change this later

Either alone is manageable — a costly-to-reverse decision made by someone sticking around can still be explained in person; a cheap decision inherited by a stranger barely matters. Both together is what raises the stakes.

items.prompt: This unit defines "legibility" as:
choices: How easily an average engineer with no prior context can read the design and correctly predict what it does
How few lines of code the design uses
How many features the design supports
How closely the design follows the latest industry trend
items.explanation: Legibility is about the reader's ability to correctly predict behavior without prior context — not brevity, feature count, or trendiness. A design can be short and still illegible (a dense one-liner nobody can parse), or long and highly legible (well-named, obvious functions).
items.reference: 👁️ Legibility = a stranger reads it and predicts behavior correctly
items.learnMore: Legibility isn't a style preference like 'clean code' — it's a testable property: hand the design to someone with zero prior context and see if they can correctly say what it does. Northlane's plain EntitlementRule array passes this test; the DSL doesn't, until the reader first learns a grammar unique to this one codebase.

items.prompt: This unit defines "cleverness" (as a design property, in the negative sense it warns about) as:
choices: A design that's more compact or general, but relies on insight only the original author reliably has
Any design that uses a design pattern
Code that has comments explaining it
A design that took a long time to build
items.explanation: Cleverness in this unit's sense is specifically about a design's understandability being bottlenecked on its author's insight — not pattern usage, comment presence, or build time. A design can use a well-known pattern and still be perfectly legible if the pattern is applied in a standard, recognizable way.
items.reference: 👁️ Legibility = a stranger reads it and predicts behavior correctly
items.learnMore: Legibility isn't a style preference like 'clean code' — it's a testable property: hand the design to someone with zero prior context and see if they can correctly say what it does. Northlane's plain EntitlementRule array passes this test; the DSL doesn't, until the reader first learns a grammar unique to this one codebase.

items.prompt: Which of these is the best one-sentence summary of the legibility-vs-cleverness trade-off this unit describes?
choices: Cleverness buys speed of change for someone who already understands the design; legibility buys speed of change for someone who doesn't
Legibility is always better, in every situation, with no trade-off at all
Cleverness is always faster to build and legibility is always slower, with no other differences
The two are unrelated to who ends up maintaining the code
items.explanation: The trade-off is specifically about who benefits from each property — a design's author gets more leverage from cleverness, while an unfamiliar future maintainer gets more leverage from legibility. Framing it as 'legibility always wins' misses that cleverness is a real, sometimes-correct trade when the design genuinely needs the extra expressiveness and the audience is known to have the context.
items.reference: 👁️ Legibility = a stranger reads it and predicts behavior correctly
items.learnMore: Legibility isn't a style preference like 'clean code' — it's a testable property: hand the design to someone with zero prior context and see if they can correctly say what it does. Northlane's plain EntitlementRule array passes this test; the DSL doesn't, until the reader first learns a grammar unique to this one codebase.

items.prompt: What does an ADR (Architecture Decision Record) capture that the code by itself does not?
choices: The reasoning behind the decision, including the alternatives that were considered and rejected, and why
A complete copy of the source code, for backup purposes
A performance benchmark of the final implementation
A list of every engineer who ever touched the file
items.explanation: Code shows what was built; it doesn't reliably preserve why one option was chosen over another that also would have worked. An ADR exists specifically to record that reasoning — including rejected alternatives — in a durable, checked-in artifact rather than in a Slack thread or someone's memory.
items.reference:
📄 Code shows what
❓ ADR shows why, including what was rejected
items.learnMore: A minimal ADR has four parts: Context (the problem and constraints), Decision (what was chosen), Rejected alternatives (what else was seriously considered and why not), and Consequences (what this makes easier, harder, or riskier later). The rejected-alternatives section is the part teams skip most, and the part that pre-empts the exact question a future engineer is most likely to ask.

items.prompt: An engineer writes a thorough design doc before building a feature, gets it approved in a review, then never looks at it again once the code ships. Is this the same thing as the ADR practice this unit describes?
choices: Not quite — an ADR is meant to be read later, by someone who wasn't in the original approval process, to answer a question that comes up after the fact
Yes, exactly the same practice under a different name
No, because ADRs must always be approved by a committee
No, because ADRs can only be written after the code ships, never before
items.explanation: A design doc written purely to get pre-approval and then abandoned misses the ADR's actual audience: a future reader, likely without any of the original context, trying to answer 'why wasn't the obvious alternative done instead.' The unit frames the ADR as a record written for that future question, not paperwork for the original decision meeting.
items.reference:
📄 Code shows what
❓ ADR shows why, including what was rejected
items.learnMore: A minimal ADR has four parts: Context (the problem and constraints), Decision (what was chosen), Rejected alternatives (what else was seriously considered and why not), and Consequences (what this makes easier, harder, or riskier later). The rejected-alternatives section is the part teams skip most, and the part that pre-empts the exact question a future engineer is most likely to ask.

items.prompt: In the one-way-door / two-way-door framing this unit uses, a "two-way door" decision is one that:
choices: Is cheap to reverse if it turns out to be wrong
Requires two separate teams to approve it
Always involves a user-facing feature
Can never be changed once it ships
items.explanation: A two-way door is defined purely by reversal cost being low — it has nothing to do with approval process, user-facingness, or permanence (that's the one-way door's definition, the opposite of this one).
items.reference:
🚪↔️ Two-way: walk back through, low cost
🚪➡️ One-way: a real commitment, once taken
items.learnMore: This framing (popularized by Amazon's leadership principles) exists to help a decider calibrate how much process a decision deserves before committing, not to judge decisions after the fact. A two-way door can usually be decided quickly and adjusted later; a one-way door earns a slower, more deliberate process precisely because getting it wrong is expensive to fix.

items.prompt: What does this unit say a one-way door decision deserves, compared to a two-way door decision?
choices: More scrutiny and caution before committing — a second opinion, more deliberate review
Exactly the same amount of process, since all decisions are equally important
Less scrutiny, since it will be reversed less often anyway
No documentation, since it won't change again
items.explanation: The framing exists specifically to allocate scrutiny in proportion to reversal cost — one-way doors earn more caution up front because getting them wrong is expensive to fix, while two-way doors can be decided quickly since a wrong call is cheap to correct.
items.reference:
🚪↔️ Two-way: walk back through, low cost
🚪➡️ One-way: a real commitment, once taken
items.learnMore: This framing (popularized by Amazon's leadership principles) exists to help a decider calibrate how much process a decision deserves before committing, not to judge decisions after the fact. A two-way door can usually be decided quickly and adjusted later; a one-way door earns a slower, more deliberate process precisely because getting it wrong is expensive to fix.

items.prompt: Renata's rule-engine DSL looks, in isolation, like a swappable implementation detail. What does this unit say actually determines whether it's a one-way or two-way door?
choices: Whether other things (like config written by other services) come to depend on the DSL's specific syntax, not just whether the code itself could technically be rewritten
How many lines of code the interpreter has
Whether Renata personally likes the design
Whether it was reviewed by a senior engineer before merging
items.explanation: Door type isn't a property of the code's rewritability in isolation — it's a property of what has come to depend on it. A DSL's syntax becomes a contract the moment other parties write config in it, even though the interpreter code itself could technically always be deleted.
items.reference:

🚪➡️ One-way: a real commitment, once taken

A two-way door can usually be decided quickly and adjusted later; a one-way door earns a slower, more deliberate process precisely because getting it wrong is expensive to fix.

items.prompt: This unit defines "lock-in" as:
choices: The state where reversing a decision now costs far more than making it did
Any decision that was approved by management
A decision that uses a proprietary vendor tool
A bug that was never fixed
items.explanation: Lock-in is specifically about the gap between original cost and current reversal cost — not approval source, vendor choice, or bug status. A decision can lock a team in without any vendor involved (Renata's own in-house DSL is the example used).
items.reference: 📈 Lock-in = reversal cost climbing above original cost
items.learnMore: Lock-in isn't a binary state a decision has or doesn't — it's a growing gap. On day one a decision might be nearly free to reverse; the same decision, unreversed for eight months while more things depend on it, can become functionally permanent, without the decision itself ever changing.

items.prompt: According to this unit, when does the real risk of a one-way-door decision typically materialize?
choices: Later — after the decision ships, as more things come to depend on it, not at the moment it's made
Immediately, the instant the code merges
It never materializes if the code passes its tests
Only if the original author leaves the company
items.explanation: The unit is explicit that lock-in's cost arrives on a delay — the decision has near-zero dependents on day one, and the cost of reversing it climbs as adoption grows, which is exactly why the decision deserves scrutiny while it's still cheap to walk back rather than after the fact.
items.reference: 📈 Lock-in = reversal cost climbing above original cost
items.learnMore: Lock-in isn't a binary state a decision has or doesn't — it's a growing gap. On day one a decision might be nearly free to reverse; the same decision, unreversed for eight months while more things depend on it, can become functionally permanent, without the decision itself ever changing.

items.prompt: Northlane's DSL has zero dependents on the day it ships, and 40 stored config strings written against it eight months later. What changed about the underlying decision itself between those two points?
choices: Nothing about the decision changed — only what depends on it changed, which is what raised the reversal cost
The decision itself became a worse design over those eight months
The code got objectively buggier over time
Nothing changed at all, including the reversal cost
items.explanation: Lock-in isn't about the decision degrading in quality — the DSL is exactly as well-built at month 8 as it was on day one. What changed is the surrounding dependency surface, and that surface, not the decision's intrinsic quality, is what determines reversal cost.
items.reference: 📈 Lock-in = reversal cost climbing above original cost
items.learnMore: Lock-in isn't a binary state a decision has or doesn't — it's a growing gap. On day one a decision might be nearly free to reverse; the same decision, unreversed for eight months while more things depend on it, can become functionally permanent, without the decision itself ever changing.

items.prompt: L2 argues that "it works, and all tests pass" is not a sufficient bar for a long-outliving design decision. Why not?
choices: Because 'works' only measures the present, while the decision's real cost shows up later, in a future where the original author may not be available to help
Because passing tests is never a meaningful signal of correctness
Because every design must be rewritten eventually regardless of quality
Because staff engineers are held to a different testing standard than everyone else
items.explanation: Tests passing is a real, meaningful signal about current correctness — the unit isn't dismissing that. The gap it points to is temporal: 'works' is a present-tense measurement, but the risk this unit is about (a stranger inheriting the design without context) only shows up later, which tests taken today can't measure.
items.reference:
✅ "Works" = present-tense
🔮 Long-term risk = shows up later, when the author's gone
items.learnMore: L2 reframes the question this way: not 'what's the best design I can build,' but 'what's the best design a stranger, arriving after I'm gone, can safely operate and extend.' A design can score perfectly on the first question and poorly on the second — Renata's DSL is exactly that case.

items.prompt: L2 says a design that "requires its original author's memory to safely extend" hasn't actually solved the long-term version of the problem. What has it done instead?
choices: Deferred a chunk of the cost onto whoever inherits it, who pays it with less context and less help than the author currently has
Solved the problem completely, just more slowly than expected
Made the problem permanently unsolvable
Transferred the cost to the company's finance department
items.explanation: The unit frames this as cost deferral, not cost elimination or an unrelated transfer — the total work of maintaining the design doesn't shrink, it just moves in time to a person with strictly worse conditions (less context, less access to the original author) than the person who built it.
items.reference:
✅ "Works" = present-tense
🔮 Long-term risk = shows up later, when the author's gone
items.learnMore: L2 reframes the question this way: not 'what's the best design I can build,' but 'what's the best design a stranger, arriving after I'm gone, can safely operate and extend.' A design can score perfectly on the first question and poorly on the second — Renata's DSL is exactly that case.

items.prompt: L2 says the question that decides between legibility and cleverness is:
choices: Who, on average, is going to be doing the changing to this design
Which option took less time to build
Which option the original author personally prefers
Which option has fewer total characters of code
items.explanation: The deciding question is about the audience for future changes, not build time, personal preference, or raw size. For a design meant to outlive its author, that audience is usually someone without the author's context — which is what tips the trade toward legibility.
items.reference: 🙋 Who does the changing, on average, over this design's life?
items.learnMore: This question is deliberately about the average future editor, not the current author. Renata could correctly note she personally finds the DSL easy to extend — that's true and irrelevant, since she won't be the one extending it two years from now.

Nothing — more powerful always means better, without exception
Power is irrelevant to design quality in every case
The DSL isn't actually more powerful than the plain version
items.explanation: L2 explicitly separates 'what can this design express' (power) from 'who can safely change what it already expresses' (legibility) — the two aren't the same axis, and buying more of one at the cost of the other is only a good trade if the extra power answers a real, current requirement rather than a speculative one.

items.learnMore: This question is deliberately about the average future editor, not the current author. Renata could correctly note she personally finds the DSL easy to extend — that's true and irrelevant, since she won't be the one extending it two years from now.

items.prompt: L3's failure-mode table describes "over-applying legible over clever" as a real risk. What does that failure mode actually look like?
choices: Rejecting a genuinely necessary abstraction because it's "too clever," and ending up with something worse, like an unmanageable if/else block nobody can hold in their head either
Writing code with too many comments
Using TypeScript instead of JavaScript
Choosing a design that's slightly more expensive than necessary
items.explanation: The failure mode L3 names is specifically over-correcting toward simplicity when the problem genuinely needs more structure — the result (a giant unmanageable conditional) isn't actually legible either, it's just simple-looking while being just as hard to safely change.
items.reference: ⚠️ "Simple" isn't automatically legible if it doesn't fit the real problem
items.learnMore: L3's guard against this failure mode: legibility is about matching complexity to the real problem, not minimizing complexity unconditionally. A design that's simple but wrong for the actual requirement isn't legible — it's under-built, which creates its own kind of illegibility (a huge conditional nobody can trace).

items.prompt: L3's failure-mode table lists "designing for a future reader who never appears" as a risk. What does it warn happens in that case?
choices: Speculative flexibility gets added for an imagined future need that never materializes, and everyone pays its complexity cost forever anyway
The design becomes too legible and too easy for beginners to understand
The original author is fired for over-engineering
Nothing bad happens — extra flexibility is always free
items.explanation: This failure mode is the mirror image of building the DSL prematurely: adding generality 'for whoever inherits this' before a second concrete case actually justifies it means paying the complexity cost immediately for a benefit that may never be collected, since the imagined future reader's need never shows up.

items.prompt: Which specific part of Northlane's decision does L3's ADR identify as the actual one-way door — not "having a rule engine" in general, but the precise thing that becomes hard to reverse?
choices: The DSL's syntax itself, once other services start writing stored config strings against it
The choice of TypeScript as the implementation language
The decision to write any automated tests at all
The decision to use an array data structure
items.explanation: The ADR's rejected-alternatives reasoning is precise about this: it's not code architecture in the abstract that locks the team in, it's the DSL's specific syntax becoming a contract the moment config strings are written against it by other parties — reversing after that means migrating every stored string, not just editing one file.
items.reference: 🔒 The one-way part: the DSL's syntax, once written elsewhere
items.learnMore: Being precise about exactly what part of a decision is the one-way component (versus what's still freely changeable) is itself a design skill — most decisions are a bundle of choices, only some of which actually lock the team in.

items.prompt: Suppose Northlane later exposes entitlement rules through a public API that other internal teams' services call directly (not just read from a database). Compared to before that API existed, what happens to the rules array's door type?
choices: It can shift toward one-way, since other services now depend on the API's shape and behavior, even though the underlying array was always a two-way-door implementation detail
Nothing changes — implementation details never affect door type
It becomes impossible to ever change the rules again, permanently
It automatically becomes a two-way door, since APIs are always safer than DSLs
items.explanation: This tests the general principle, not just the DSL-specific case: door type isn't fixed to a design forever — it tracks what currently depends on it. An internal array with no external dependents is two-way; the same array, once exposed via an API other services call directly, gains real external dependents on its behavior and shifts toward needing one-way-door caution for future changes, even without any DSL involved.

items.prompt: L3's first extend-it question asks what happens if Northlane grows to 40 engineers across 6 teams all touching entitlement rules. What tension does that scenario introduce for Option B specifically?
choices: The review-and-deploy cost per change, cheap at 6 engineers, may start to look more like the DSL's config-time flexibility becomes attractive again — for coordination reasons, not urgency reasons
Option B stops compiling once more than 6 engineers use it
There is no tension — Option B scales identically regardless of team size
Enterprise tier customers would immediately churn
items.explanation: The question is designed to show the worked example is one case, not the whole territory: at larger scale, the review/deploy cost that was clearly worth paying at 6 engineers might become a real coordination bottleneck across 6 teams, which could tip the calculus back toward some form of config-time flexibility — for a different reason (throughput across many teams) than the same-day-urgency case already addressed.
items.reference: 📈 Scale changes which cost is the bottleneck
items.learnMore: This is the point of L3's closing extend-it questions: Renata's decision was correct for her specific inputs (6 engineers, a few changes per quarter), not universally correct. A good decider re-runs the same reasoning process against new inputs rather than treating the prior conclusion as a fixed rule.

items.prompt: L3's second extend-it question imagines the DSL had already shipped to production for three months, with three services depending on it, before the ADR was raised. What does the question suggest changes about the ADR's job in that scenario?
choices: It shifts from choosing the design up front to documenting the cost of migrating off an already-adopted one-way door, which is a different (and harder) kind of decision
Nothing changes — the ADR's job is identical regardless of timing
The ADR becomes unnecessary once code has shipped to production
The decision must legally stay with the DSL forever once shipped
items.explanation: The question is deliberately open-ended, but the shift it points at is real: once dependents already exist, the decision is no longer 'which design to build' — it's 'is migrating off the now-adopted one-way door worth its cost,' a genuinely different and usually harder calculation than the original choice would have been, made before any lock-in had accrued.
